newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish think-tank says EMU negative in short term.
newsitem.headline: Swedish think-tank says EMU negative in short term.

text.p: A Swedish government think-tank set up to examine the consequences of possible participation in the single currency of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union said on Monday arguments against joining the first round of the EMU prevailed.
Swedish think-tank says EMU negative in short term

"Our overall evaluation of both economic and political arguments is that the factors that speak against Swedish participation in the first round in 1999 are stronger than those that support it," the government's Calmfors commission said in its final report.
However, the commission said it was more positive to Swedish participation in the single currency in the longer term.

"Any Swedish decision not join in 1999 should be formulated as if we aim to take part later on when the conditions are right," the report said, adding that it would want unemployment to fall and state finances to stabilise before wholeheartedly supporting membership.
The commission said it was not possible to draw any definitive conclusions in the EMU issue.
"Any stance is dependent on valuations of how important different consequences may be, and on uncertain judgements of the future under different alternatives," it said.
One argument supporting Swedish participation in the currency union is efficiency, the commission said.
Swedish think-tank says EMU negative in short term

One positive effect could be a faster fall in long real interest rates than would otherwise be the case, it said, but added that the balance of economic arguments were currently against participation.

"For Sweden's part, we believe that the costs of stabilisation policy associated with a common currency are greater than the benefits. Even temporary macro-economic disruption could have lasting effects on production and employment if they are not counteracted."
The commission said that economic fundamentals suggested that Sweden sould retain its existing monetary policy strategy with a floating exchange rate and an inflation target.

"We see considerable risks in participation in an ERM (exchange rate mechanism) system in which economic policy may once again need to be directed to defending an exchange rate target," the Calmfors commission said.
